consensus_snapshot: Within the PE dataset, BiLSTM-CRF-CNN sequence tagging with distance labels (STagBLCC) and an adapted LSTM-ER achieve performance comparable to or exceeding the Stab & Gurevych (2016) ILP baseline at paragraph granularity (supported by Table 1 and Experiments §5).

Explicitly encoding inter-component distance into tagging labels is an effective inductive bias on PE, aligning model predictions with the dataset's short-range relation distribution and improving relation identification on longer essays (supported by Models §4 Eq.1, Data §3 Figure 2, and Figure 4).
Dependency-parsing framings (the evaluated parsers) underperform the best tagging approaches in the presented PE experiments and degrade more when moving from paragraph to essay granularity.
Adding component/relation auxiliary subtasks in a multi-task configuration yields modest improvements (a few percentage points) under the reported experimental setup.
disagreement_snapshot: Extent of generalization: reviewers disagree on how strongly PE-based results support broader claims; some view dataset-dependence as a major limitation requiring cross-dataset validation, others see the paper as a meaningful empirical consolidation whose claims should be explicitly scoped.

Cause of LSTM-ER relation degradation at essay level: reviewers are split between accepting the combinatorial candidate-explosion explanation as plausible and insisting that alternative causes (hyperparameter/tuning, class imbalance) must be experimentally ruled out.

Severity of parser underperformance: some reviewers attribute parser weakness to inherent framing mismatch for AM, while others attribute part of the gap to resource/tuning constraints (parsers trained paragraph-only) and recommend re-evaluation with parity in tuning/training regimes.
uncertainty_snapshot: Dataset representativeness: PE's strong short-distance and paragraph-localization properties create epistemic uncertainty about transfer of methods (especially distance-encoded tagging) to domains where relations are more long-range or cross-paragraph (shared_analysis A1/A2).

Granularity comparability: models trained at different document granularities (paragraph vs essay) create uncertainty in claims about scalability and relative performance on long texts (shared_analysis A3).

Mechanistic attribution: absence of targeted ablations (gold-component feeding, candidate pruning, distance-bucketing experiments) makes causal claims about why certain framings win uncertain (shared_analysis M3/M4).

Reproducibility details: hyperparameter search parity, random-seed variance reporting, and explicit distance-label handling are not fully present in the main text, limiting replication and confidence in whether differences stem from modeling choices or optimization effort (shared_analysis A5).

Before elevating broad claims about replacing ILP/feature engineering, require the authors to (a) add targeted ablations that isolate causal mechanisms (gold-component-to-relation tests, candidate pruning for LSTM-ER, distance-bucketing experiments), (b) resolve or explicitly partition comparisons by training granularity so that paragraph-only results are not conflated with essay-level claims, and (c) improve reproducibility transparency (summarize hyperparameter searches, report variance, detail distance encoding). If authors cannot run cross-dataset experiments, they must significantly temper generalization language and clearly state PE-specific scope. The editor should not treat this as a theoretical advance but as an empirical/engineering consolidation; revisions should focus on the ablations and transparency items listed rather than on wholesale new methods.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen claims and practicality, prioritize the following revisions or additional results: 1) Provide exact details and statistics for the distance label d (range/clipping/bucketing, label-set size, per-label train/dev/test counts) and add an ablation comparing raw vs clipped/bucketed encodings. 2) Run targeted ablations: (i) feed gold component spans to relation modules for both LSTM-ER and tagging-based approaches to separate detection vs relation-classification errors; (ii) implement candidate-pruning (distance threshold, paragraph-based restriction, learned priors) for LSTM-ER and report essay-level R-F1 to test the combinatorial-explosion hypothesis; (iii) optionally add a variant of LSTM-ER with an explicit distance feature to assess impact. 3) Where feasible, retrain or evaluate key models under matched training granularity (paragraph-only and essay-only) and present matched comparisons; if resource-limited, clearly separate paragraph-level and essay-level experimental blocks and avoid cross-granularity aggregation. 4) Expand baseline diversity or qualify comparative claims: add at least one additional engineered baseline (e.g., Persing & Ng variant) or clearly state that ILP comparison is to Stab & Gurevych (2016) only. 5) Improve reproducibility: summarize hyperparameter search ranges and budgets, publish random seeds and mean±std over multiple runs for main metrics, and release code/configs for main experiments. 6) Soften generalization statements if cross-dataset tests are not added, explicitly framing recommendations as PE-conditional.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
This empirical study systematically compares multiple neural end-to-end framings for argumentation mining on the Persuasive Essays dataset. It finds that BiLSTM-CRF-CNN sequence tagging augmented with an explicit inter-component distance label (STagBLCC) and an adapted LSTM-ER entity-relation model perform at or above a prior ILP baseline at paragraph granularity; tagging with distance labels helps relation identification at essay granularity; dependency-parsing framings evaluated perform worse in these experiments; and multi-task inclusion of component/relation subtasks gives modest gains.

Strengths:
- Extensive head-to-head experiments across parsers, taggers (including BLCC), MTL variants, and LSTM-ER using Persing & Ng metrics, plus interpretable diagnostics (distance distributions and relation-distance correctness).
- Pragmatic novelty: encoding relation distance in tagging labels (Eq.1) is simple and effective on PE.
- Actionable recommendations about framing choices depending on document length and modularity needs.

Limitations:
- Heavy reliance on the Persuasive Essays dataset (short paragraphs and skewed short-distance relations) limits external validity; it is unclear how distance-encoding will behave on corpora with long-range or cross-paragraph relations. (Request: cross-dataset tests or explicit scoping.)
- Training-granularity mismatch: parsers trained only on paragraphs due to memory constraints while other models have essay-level evaluations; this confounds claims about scalability and relative long-document performance. (Request: matched-granularity comparisons or explicit partitioning of results.)
- Key causal explanations are correlational: no ablation isolates whether LSTM-ER relation degradation is due to candidate-combinatorics or other causes; likewise, the active role of distance-encoding is not proven via distance-bucketing/clipping ablations. (Request: targeted ablations: gold components, candidate pruning, distance bucketing.)
- Reproducibility/operational detail gap: exact handling of distance labels (range/clipping/bucketing), hyperparameter search budgets, seeds, and metric variance are not fully reported in main text and should be made explicit.

Open Questions:
- What exact distance encoding was used (max |d|, bucketing strategy)? Provide label-set size and per-d frequency distributions and an ablation of alternate encodings.
- What is the relation-classification performance when feeding gold components to the relation modules (for both LSTM-ER and tagging-derived relation extraction)? This isolates component vs relation error sources.
- Does pruning candidate relation pairs for LSTM-ER (distance threshold, paragraph-restriction, learned prior) recover essay-level R-F1? Please run/prioritize these experiments to test the combinatorial-explosion hypothesis.
- Can the main findings be reproduced on at least one additional AM dataset with different paragraph/distance statistics, or on synthetic variants of PE (e.g., merged paragraphs) to probe generalization?

Transparency:
- Supplementary material reportedly contains hyperparameter and embedding details; for clarity, include a concise main-text table summarizing tuning ranges, budgets, selected settings, number of runs, seeds and variance for core models. Explicitly state which models had access to paragraph/essay indicators and the exact distance-label operationalization. Release code and configs for key experiments.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
